objective: Recognize atypical presentations in older adults, such as delirium or falls as the first sign of infection

brief.situation: 15:30 in a family practice. You are the nurse practitioner. Mrs. Gutierrez, 84, comes with her daughter: two falls this week, and since yesterday she is 'not herself', mixing up her grandchildren's names. No cough she mentions, no fever at home.
handover: Hypertension on lisinopril; mild osteoarthritis. Lives with her daughter; walks with a cane; sharp and independent until this week.
The medical assistant has a urine dipstick ready and says, 'Probably a UTI, they always are at her age.'
Practice policy: an older adult with signs of sepsis or new hypoxia goes to the emergency department the same visit; the hospital is 10 minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the falls and confusion are telling you.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Pneumonia with early sepsis worsens slowly through the visit. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of septic shock in the clinic. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The emergency referral decided within 10 minutes of the first finding of infection (practice policy).
Calling the emergency department and an ambulance, and the hand-over: about 15 min.

A change since yesterday that comes and goes; can't name the days backward; drifts between topics. Positive: delirium, not her baseline.
Crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base. Abdomen soft, no suprapubic tenderness. Bruised left hip, no deformity.
Leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative. She has no burning, frequency or urgency.
No new medicines, no sedatives. Standing makes her lightheaded; the systolic drops 14.

why.question: What is causing Mrs. Gutierrez's falls and confusion, and what does the dipstick tell you?

parts.label: What it is
parts.criteria: New delirium and falls in an 84-year-old are an atypical presentation of acute illness; a counted respiratory rate over 22, new hypoxia, a temperature above her baseline and right basal crackles point to pneumonia with early sepsis.
parts.modelAnswer: New confusion and falls in a sharp 84-year-old are how infection often presents at her age. Her breathing is fast, her saturation is low, she is warm for her, and she has crackles at the right base: pneumonia with early sepsis.

parts.label: The dipstick and the plan
parts.criteria: A positive dipstick without urinary symptoms is likely asymptomatic bacteriuria, not the cause; delirium without urinary symptoms is investigated for other causes; emergency department now.
parts.modelAnswer: The dipstick is positive but she has no urinary symptoms; at her age that is usually asymptomatic bacteriuria, and treating it would miss the pneumonia. She goes to the emergency department now.

shock.headline: Shock in the exam room
shock.body: In older adults, falls and new confusion can be the first sign of infection. Count the respiratory rate and check SpO2 early.

home.headline: Home with the wrong diagnosis
home.body: A positive dipstick without urinary symptoms is usually asymptomatic bacteriuria; investigate other causes of delirium. Falls are not explained by bacteriuria.

edNow.headline: Atypical presentation caught
edNow.body: You counted the breathing, screened for delirium, found the crackles and sent her the same visit. That is the expert path.

edGaps.headline: Sent, with gaps
edGaps.body: Check how long the decision took and whether delirium and the lungs were examined.

time_up.headline: Still in the exam room
time_up.body: Early sepsis in an older adult needs a decision within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Two falls and new, fluctuating confusion in a previously sharp 84-year-old are an atypical presentation of acute illness. A counted respiratory rate of 23, an SpO2 of 91%, a temperature well above her usual and right basal crackles point to pneumonia with early sepsis. The positive dipstick without urinary symptoms is likely asymptomatic bacteriuria: guidance advises investigating other causes of delirium first, and falls are not explained by bacteriuria. She goes to the emergency department now.
